details:
**The Swing**
Jean-Honoré Fragonard's 1767 painting, the definitive Rococo image. A woman in a pink dress and straw hat swings in a garden and kicks off her slipper, while a young man hiding in the bushes below looks up her skirt. An older man pushes the swing from behind. The patron's original request was for a bishop to push the swing, but in the finished painting the figure is usually read as a cuckolded husband.

**Cupid statue with finger to lips**
In The Swing, a statue of Cupid on the left puts his finger to his lips, urging silence and secrecy about the flirtation taking place below.

**The Embarkation for Cythera**
Antoine Watteau's 1717 painting of elegant couples beside a golden boat with cherubs (putti) flying overhead and a rose-covered statue of Venus on the right. Cythera is the island sacred to Aphrodite (Venus), and scholars debate whether the couples are arriving or leaving.

**Fête galante**
A genre of painting invented by Watteau, showing aristocrats in fancy dress enjoying amorous outdoor leisure in idyllic parkland. The French Academy created the category to admit Watteau with The Embarkation for Cythera.

**Jean-Antoine Watteau**
The French painter who launched Rococo painting. Besides the Embarkation, he painted Pierrot (formerly called Gilles), a life-size image of the commedia dell'arte clown standing in white in front of other stock characters.

**Jean-Honoré Fragonard**
A student of François Boucher and the last great Rococo painter. His works include The Swing, The Stolen Kiss (a youth secretly kissing a young woman holding a striped shawl), and The Progress of Love series.

**François Boucher**
A leading Rococo painter and favorite of Madame de Pompadour. He painted The Toilette of Venus, in which a nude Venus holds a dove while cherubs attend her (one reaches for a pearl necklace), and Diana Leaving Her Bath, also called Diana After the Hunt. He also decorated parts of the Hôtel de Soubise in Paris and helped popularize chinoiserie.

**Blonde Odalisque / Diderot**
Boucher painted Marie-Louise O'Murphy, a teenage mistress of Louis XV, lying nude on her stomach. The critic Denis Diderot attacked Boucher's erotic subjects, and he accused him of "prostituting his own wife" by using her as the model for a similar odalisque.

**Madame de Pompadour**
The influential mistress of Louis XV, who was a major patron of Rococo art and helped popularize the style. Boucher painted several portraits of her, and he painted The Toilette of Venus for her château at Bellevue.

**Jupiter and Callisto**
Boucher painted several versions of the myth in which Jupiter disguises himself as the goddess Diana to seduce the nymph Callisto, with putti flying around them.

**The Progress of Love**
A series by Fragonard commissioned for Madame du Barry, who rejected it. Its panels include The Pursuit, The Meeting, The Lover Crowned, and Love Letters, in which two lovers read letters with a dog at their feet. The series is now at the Frick Collection in New York.

**Clodion**
Claude Michel, known as Clodion, was the leading Rococo sculptor. He made small, playful terracotta works with bacchanalian themes, such as Nymph and Satyr Carousing and the reliefs The Intoxication of Wine and Faun Family.

**Giovanni Battista Tiepolo**
The great Venetian Rococo fresco painter. He decorated the Würzburg Residence in Germany and painted The Apotheosis of Spain on the ceiling of the Royal Palace of Madrid.

**Thomas Chippendale**
An English cabinetmaker whose furniture designs, published in The Gentleman and Cabinet-Maker's Director, mixed Rococo, Gothic, and Chinese motifs and helped popularize the style in England.

**Pilgrimage Church of Wies**
A Bavarian church designed by Dominikus Zimmermann, considered a masterpiece of Rococo architecture for its white-and-gold interior full of light and ornate stucco.
